article.title: Can the Boss’s Technology Dismantle the Boss’s Penthouse?A Case for Ecological Operaismo
article.author: Socialist Forum
article.content: “The smarter our life, the less control we have over it.” —Jathan Sadowski [1] In a world where Big Tech too often sets the terms and conditions of basic human interaction within and beyond the workplace, more and more people are wondering how many of the supposedly “necessary” or “inevitable” algorithmic technologies we really need. Is it even possible for this digital machinery to serve the long-term interests of the many instead of the short-term interests of the few? For French Marxist philosopher and first-wave eco-socialist André Gorz, the answer, in many cases, was no. “It is only because capital needs consumers for its products that production also serves human needs,” he wrote. But “they are needs and desires which have been produced to satisfy capital’s need for profitability.” [2] With a nod to Gorz, one way to think about eco-socialism in the twenty-first century is as a three-pronged, transnational revolutionary project to do the following: democratically redefine basic human and nonhuman needs — including subsistence needs, occupational needs, and communicative needs — in opposition to the narrowly defined, market-driven needs of the owner-investor class; [3] radically reconfigure society so that it’s possible to universally satisfy everyone’s (overlapping but variable) needs within the biophysical constraints of the planet, thus repairing what second-wave eco-socialists call the “metabolic rift” between sociotechnical systems and socioecological systems; and liberate the free, creative, self-directed development of human and nonhuman potential from the constraints of capital. [4] In what follows, I argue that an “ecological operaismo ” — envisioned here as a fusion between autonomist Marxism (Italian workerism) and degrowth economics — can be one way for socialists to understand and ultimately transform the webs of social, ecological, and technological relations so as to decrease alienation (from self, society, labor, and nature) and increase workers’ collective ability to assert more direct, democratic control over our time and our space, our working conditions and our living conditions. [5] To make this argument, I first analyze some of the specific, present-tense effects of chatbots, a.k.a. large language models (LLMs) or generative AI, on the living and working conditions of one particular unionized workforce — me and my fellow contingent writing teachers at a mid-size public research university in Montana. I then reflect on what this analysis reveals about the potential (or lack thereof) for chatbots to be reappropriated by education workers in a way that serves eco-socialist ends instead of capitalist ones. As Christian Fuchs explains, “to appropriate technology means attempting to turn it from a means of domination and exploitation into a means of struggle and commoning.” [6] In the process, I raise a set of questions that workers in any sector might use to guide their assessment of the degree to which a given technology’s alienating, anti-democratic effects are (or aren’t) immanent or intrinsic — that is, hard-wired into the technology itself. And I consider how to persuade historically productivist groups like the building trades [7] to be more receptive to an anti-Promethean, ecological operaismo (without resorting to what some have called “green moralizing”). Growth for the 99 percent Degrowth has some good ideas but bad PR. It’s easy to see why some on the left have derided it as a politically radioactive form of eco-austerity “rooted in the carbon guilt of the professional class.” [8] As solar communism advocate Jason Schwartzman cautions, degrowth can easily sound like “an undifferentiated attack on the standard of living and livelihood of many groups of people, especially [the] broad low-income sectors of society” who already lack access to basic necessities. [9] Branding problems aside, the useful part of degrowth is closer to what I would call “growth for the 99 percent” or “de-alienation.” [10] It starts from the premise that capitalism is a profoundly wasteful, inefficient (not to mention ecocidal) system, one characterized not only by a ravenously unsustainable appetite for space, energy, and materials, but also by wasted human potential and stunted social development. The artificial scarcity of basic survival needs, moreover, is a structural feature of compulsory commodity production (and the care work that sustains it). [11] As media studies scholar Gavin Mueller explains in Breaking Things at Work: The Luddites Were Right about Why You Hate Your Job , degrowth — also called “decelerationism” — is not a Romantic, primitivist, or ascetic “withdrawal to a slower pace of life, but the manifestation of an antagonism toward the progress of elites at the expense of the rest of us.” [12] Unlike the neoliberal “abundance” rebrand, [13] then, the basic idea of an eco-socialist degrowth of the rich is that producing more of the goods and services that workers (paid or unpaid) actually want and need invariably requires producing less of the goods and services that capital wants and needs [14] (hence the climate justice movement’s distinction between elite “luxury emissions” and agrarian, indigenous, or working-class “subsistence emissions”). Not only do we live in a world of finite resources — supplies of energy and raw materials (positive externalities) are limited, [15] as is the planet’s ability to act as a sink or a sponge for waste and pollution (negative externalities) like carbon emissions. It’s also not possible, unfortunately — as the ecomodernists would like us to believe — for technological improvements alone to “decouple” the perpetual accumulation of GDP from ecological constraints. [16] Even if the most urgent environmental problem, atmospheric CO 2 , must be addressed within capitalist frameworks, it’s also true, as Socialist Forum readers well know, that workers won’t truly be free until we decouple ourselves from capital. Labor, after all, “does not need capital,” as the autonomist technology theorist Nick Dyer-Witheford writes. “Labor can dispense with the wage, and with capitalism, and find different ways to organize its own creative energy: it is potentially autonomous .” [17] This working-class need for autonomy from capital is, moreover, existential, given capital’s tendency to prioritize technologies that turbocharge its ability to exploit, control, subdue, and dispossess an always potentially rebellious labor force. [18] Such a perspective suggests that some technologies are intrinsically anti-worker — that some forms of fixed capital simply can’t be fixed. Gorz, too, made a similar argument when he suggested that much modern machinery is deliberately (and “inflexibly”) [19] designed to require alienating tasks and rhythms, whether on a Fordist assembly line, in an Amazon warehouse, [20] or in the spheres of social and ecological reproduction that are increasingly ruled by an algorithmic factory logic. [21] class struggle technologism In a 2016 article in New Technology, Work and Employment called “When Should Workers Embrace or Resist New Technology?,” Paul Edwards and Paulina Ramirez present a six-dimensional heuristic for analyzing a technology’s effects on workers. [22] Without endorsing a “strong” technological determinism or an accelerationist, Soviet-style socialism — which would put them at odds with autonomist Marxists’ emphasis on subjective working-class antagonism as the driving historical force [23] — these scholars nonetheless endorse a “weak” or “soft” determinism that, reasonably enough, sees capitalist forces of production as a source of significant social and environmental effects, however contestable those effects might be. Edwards and Ramirez are primarily interested — as am I, in this essay — in analyzing the material effects of specific technologies rather than the ideological effects of specific technological discourses . A distinction between technical artifacts and techno-ideologies is analytically useful even if, in practice, the line is always blurred. [24] For the purposes of this essay, the most relevant techno-ideologies are these: techno-optimism : techno-oligarchs and techno-feudalists will solve everyone’s problems, so just get out of their way (agency lies with bosses, owners, investors, and entrepreneurs) techno-ambivalence : most tech is intrinsically neutral — you can use it for good or for ill (responsibility offloaded onto individual users/consumers) techno-pessimism : most tech is intrinsically bad , a weapon of class war from above — the only options are refusal, sabotage, or abolition (by oppressed groups and subordinated classes) techno-autonomism : most tech is intrinsically political — a lot of it only serves the needs and interests of capital and managers, so refusal should always be on the table, but the degree to which any tech is intrinsically bad is always a contingent outcome of competing class forces (agency lies with organized workers at the points of production and social reproduction) — or, as Langdon Winner wrote in an influential essay, “to say that some technologies are inherently political is to say that certain widely accepted reasons of practical necessity . . . have tended to eclipse other sorts of moral and political reasoning” [25] (why have certain technologies come to be perceived as “useful” or “necessary” in the first place? whose interests, which forms of social organization, and which configurations of power are served by such perceptions?) Edwards and Ramirez use their checklist to analyze the Davy miner’s lamp, California’s NUMMI lean production plant, and “the internet of things” — not from capital’s perspective, as is typically done, but from workers.’ Widely applicable to a range of technical artifacts and sociotechnical systems, their heuristic is a valuable analytical tool for organized labor. In what follows, I use their fourth criterion, “immanence of the effects,” to evaluate so-called chatbots from the point of view of public-sector education workers. I examine what seem to be some of the defining, present-tense, intrinsic technical attributes and effects of chatbots, focusing on the implications for higher ed contract faculty (non-tenure-track adjuncts, lecturers, and so on) and our students. To talk about the “immanence” of chatbots’ effects means that some effects are more or less “inscribed in the technology” in a way that “either require[s] or strongly impl[ies] certain forms of social organization.” [26] For certain effects to be “immanent” means that “the nature of the physical [or algorithmic] world enables or limits what the technology can do.” [27] Granted, blaming technology for our problems — as if it’s an autonomous force with a mind of its own — can be a dangerous form of commodity fetishism that lets capitalists off the hook. [28] Sheep didn’t forcibly enclose the English countryside starting in the sixteenth century. People did. It would, therefore, be a serious mistake to treat chatbots as “discrete tools, rather than an ensemble of interconnected systems.” [29] All artifacts presuppose “an infrastructural network of technical, social, and psychological conditions, without which the machines and products do not work.” [30] Meanwhile, the growth of these networks will continue to appear uncontrollable and unstoppable only as long as workers and the public lack the organized power to significantly influence corporate decision-making around technoscientific investment. [31] But it’s also true that blaming capitalism, and only capitalism, sometimes lets technology off the hook. “The hand-mill gives you society with the feudal lord; the steam-mill gives you society with the industrial capitalist,” as Marx put it (simplifying for effect, no doubt). [32] Even if people, not sheep, were responsible for violently proletarianizing the yeomen, it was the growing market for commodified wool, specifically, that drove early capitalists’ particular need for private sheep pastures and mechanical stocking frames, each of which had undeniable effects that were both technically and socially over-determined. [33] Ultimately, what’s at stake in an analysis of a chatbot’s immanent, intrinsic, technically determined effects — especially those effects most likely to be judged by education workers to be intrinsically alienating, anti-democratic effects — is that “the more that an effect is inscribed in the technology, the more the social choice is one of ‘take it or leave it.’” [34] For workers to decide how to respond to chatbots — abolition or transformation, refusal or reclamation — we must determine if transformation or reclamation are even possible in the first place. Is there anything salvageable or redeemable about chatbots? Can they be hijacked by workers and socialists? Or are they (and their enabling social and material infrastructures) just the latest example of wasteful, socially unnecessary crap that — along with F-16s, Cybertrucks, high-tech border surveillance, etc. — most people neither want nor need and would (for ecological reasons, especially) be better off without? These are empirical questions as much as theoretical ones. To effectively identify real, context-specific openings for worker resistance (and possible reclamation), we have to get specific. Capitalism might indeed produce its own gravediggers, but not every technology is a shovel. political deskilling College writing instructors teach students a lot more than how to write. We teach students that what they say is just as important as how they say it. We insist that their own voices, experiences, and perspectives matter a great deal, and that writing can help them develop those perspectives, analyze and contextualize those experiences, and refine those voices (or tweak them to fit the situation). Writing is an inherently social activity, we say — a way of acting in the world — and our relatively intimate class sizes allow students to witness firsthand how their work affects real flesh-and-blood readers. We give them space to argue, experiment, take risks, make mistakes, and challenge authority (including our own teacherly authority), which often results in a sense of community, even solidarity. And we help them find the right questions (not the right “AI prompts”) to ask during any writing project. Questions like: Who is my audience? What do I need or expect from them? What do they need or expect from me? In short, college writing teachers guide students through the basics of collaborative inquiry, situational awareness, mediated interaction, and the ideologically charged negotiation (sometimes cooperative, sometimes conflictual) of meaning. Information literacy is obviously a big part of that. One thing this means is that I tend to be less interested in the specific answers students come up with than in the kinds of questions they ask and the process they use to explore them. “Show your work” isn’t something only math teachers say. Writing teachers say it, too. Unfortunately, as one Human Rights Watch article about the Israeli military’s use of automated target-generation tools points out, “machine learning, AI, and other proprietary algorithms, by design, do not allow for scrutiny, or show their work or decision-making processes around how outputs are generated.” [35] Similarly, chatbots and “personal AI agents” like Copilot, Claude, DeepSeek, Grok, Gemini, Muse, and ChatGPT have (at least) seven serious flaws that seem to be baked-in design features: the training data they depend on to produce their responses — forcibly acquired via mass data plunder — is a mystery to users and designers the statistical, pattern-recognizing methods they use to analyze this data is a mystery to users and designers these statistical methods depend on outsourced ghostwork (often gig-ified and traumatizing) to fine-tune the otherwise unreliable output of factual, intelligible, non-toxic responses — as Antonio Negri emphasizes: “It seems that the algorithmic machine is itself intelligent — but this is not true. It is instead open to continuous modifications by human intelligence.” [36] these methods require “ massive amounts of brute force , in computing power and therefore in energy consumption” [37] (MSU-Bozeman’s Tempest Research Cluster, a “high performance computing (HPC)” facility, is apparently the state’s largest supercomputer) [38] their “ inherent directive to assist makes AI chatbots susceptible to manipulation through ambiguous or manipulative language” (per IBM) [39] their “tendency to make up facts [as well as sources and quotations], to double-down on incorrect information, and to perform tasks incorrectly” — called hallucinating , which some researchers consider to be an “innate” feature of LLMs [40] — “can lead to the degradation of overall information quality and further reduce veracity of and trust in freely available information” (per OpenAI), [41] a problem that platforms like Facebook have, of course, already been contributing to for many years [42] “dependency on [LLMs]” — whether voluntary or coerced — “may hinder the development of new skills or even lead to the loss of important skills ” (also per OpenAI, a company that’s adept at criticizing the same problems it created) [43] — note the contrast between this statement and my university’s “Information about Generative AI” webpage, which claims that “prohibiting student use of generative AI in courses may deprive them of valuable opportunities to develop skills and expertise in an emerging technology, which can benefit students in professions and industries that are leveraging generative AI to complete work and improve efficiency” [44] (meanwhile, our computer science department’s [45] “Social & Ethical Issues in Computer Science” course recently received an ominous rebrand: it’s now called “AI for Everyone”; it does still cover social, ethical, and legal implications, but it also now involves “learn[ing] to collaborate more effectively with AI”) [46] In a nutshell, then: chatbots seem to be, by definition , unaccountable, people-pleasing black boxes premised on the monopolization of data and on instrumentalist, Promethean relations to nonhuman nature — black boxes that, instead of reducing overall drudgery, merely outsource it to earlier and/or more distant stages in the supply chain (such as the Congo’s lithium miners or Kenya’s data labelers), [47] which makes them inherently labor-eating or labor-displacing , not “labor-saving.” [48] It certainly doesn’t help that chatbots often give inaccurate accounts of their own inaccuracies. That labor-eating technical attribute is key. The technology simply can’t work without a constant supply of alienated human labor to satiate its infinite data appetite and prevent it from developing a kind of digital mad cow disease. As Josh Dzieza explains in a damning exposé of the new white-collar gig economy, “when AI trains on AI-generated data, it gradually degrades, a phenomenon researchers call ‘model collapse.’” [49] This fact alone poses a serious problem not only for left-wing accelerationist dreams of “fully automated luxury communism,” but also for those techno-capitalists for whom “current forms of algorithmically-managed gig work are conceived as a prelude to an automated distribution network in which today’s gig workers are rendered redundant through the firm’s development and deployment of in-house technology.” [50] The subject line of an email I recently received from OpenAI was: “Use ChatGPT to make life easier.” Easier for whom and at whose expense was not specified. Even with public, democratic ownership and control, could human-powered chatbots ever not be a form of “fauxtomation” or “Potemkin AI” — that is, “services that purport to be powered by sophisticated software, but actually rely on humans acting like robots”? [51] It’s hard to see how. The phenomenon of “model collapse” suggests that a chabot could never be self-sufficient. (The best visual metaphor for AI ghostwork that I can think of is a detail from Bong Joon Ho’s 2019 movie Parasite . A series of overhead lights in a high-end house seemingly turn on automatically whenever the owner walks down the hallway. Later, we learn there’s an elderly working-class guy living in the basement who slams his forehead against a row of lightswitches whenever he hears the owner’s footsteps.) Many college students, of course, are aspiring middle-class professionals of one kind or another. And yet white-collar jobs in the so-called knowledge sectors are (like blue-collar manufacturing jobs before them) the ones that are most vulnerable to deskilling, outsourcing, and gig-ification via the ruling-class imposition of automated text and content generators. This development could inflect professional-class politics in several ways. [52] One possibility is that aspiring professionals turn inward in a desperate attempt to defend their diminishing professional-class perks and status (and, by extension, the class hierarchy that underwrites those perks and status). Another possibility is that they turn outward, organizing with low-wage workers across sectors in a more radical effort to contest the whole idea that a hierarchical, professionalized division of labor is just or necessary at all, and to insist that everyone , not just credentialed white-collar workers, is entitled to respect, security, [53] autonomy, humane treatment, a living wage, leisure time, a clean and healthy environment, and meaningful control over the shape and texture of their work and everyday lives — including access to the basic means of survival (food, housing, health care, transportation, education, communication, etc.). [54] The second option is, from a socialist perspective, clearly preferable. My concern is that, because a chatbot’s ostensibly factual, descriptive statements are structurally detached from the reality it’s pretending to describe or know about, algorithmic text generators don’t just alienate workers from the means of survival. By further monopolizing control over knowledge and information and imposing artificial, commodified scarcity on what should be public, collective resources, they also alienate workers from the means of learning about the means of survival. Chatbots prey on my students’ desire to learn about how the world works, and about what role they can or should play in social, civic, and economic life. This amounts to a kind of political deskilling : the systematic deprivation of the dialectical, human-generated forms of knowledge and information that are needed to understand how capitalism works, and how to change it. The knowledge produced by the natural and social sciences is always an interpretation of the world, of course. But, at least from a materialist perspective, the usefulness and accuracy of this knowledge — however partial and provisional it might be — is always constrained by material contexts and concrete human activities. “All social life is essentially practical,” as Karl Marx wrote. “All the mysteries which lead theory towards mysticism find their rational solution in human practice and in the comprehension of this practice.” [55] A chatbot is a mystical tool — one designed according to idealist (rather than materialist) specifications. Its outputs are epistemically detached from the concrete worlds its users are trying to understand and intervene in. If you ask a chatbot to summarize, say, The Communist Manifesto , what you’ll get is not the SparkNotes version of The Communist Manifesto . You’ll get the statistical average of how millions of other people (across the political spectrum) have summarized The Communist Manifesto . You’ll get, not the SparkNotes version, but the SparkNotes version of a million other SparkNotes versions. In other words: bullshit. [56] To reduce the concrete, qualitative labor of human writers to abstract, quantitative statistical patterns is a textbook example of alienation, whereby “workers not only experience their product as alien but also the various machines, tools, and spaces used to create those products.” [57] Indeed, as computational linguists Emily Bender and Alexander Koller emphasize, “meaning” is not a property of textual form alone. Meaning emerges from the socially, materially situated interplay between embodied writers/speakers and readers/listeners. Meaning presupposes a reader/listener who can use “their own knowledge of the communicative situation and their hypotheses about the speaker’s state of mind and intention.” Because a chatbot “only uses form as training data,” it “cannot in principle lead to learning of meaning,” which derives from (always situated and evolving) human needs, goals, and intentions. Indeed, “the slogan ‘meaning is use’ (often attributed to Wittgenstein) . . . refers not to ‘use’ as ‘distribution in a text corpus’ but rather [to the idea] that language is used in the real world to convey communicative intents to real people.” [58] To say that a chatbot is capable of understanding what you typed (or the context around it) is like saying that a piece of paper is capable of understanding what you scribbled. Chatbots can thus be viewed as capital’s attempt to steal back from workers — to reappropriate, to disembody — the embodied forms of fixed cognitive capital that, according to Negri, workers themselves had previously appropriated and internalized. Indeed, workers’ accumulated mental and creative capacities are what make them a potentially insurgent, autonomous agent. [59] “Smart” devices, by contrast, are containers for dead labor, and the ecologically unsustainable growth of dead labor poses an existential threat to living labor. In algorithmic capitalism, the class struggle is truly life-and-death: living labor struggles to reanimate (by re-embodying) dead labor; capital, meanwhile, does the opposite, as it struggles to control, exploit, and disrupt this process whenever it can — hence Big Tech’s mass injection of chatbots into schools, one of the primary social sites where people are given the chance to have their minds and bodies imprinted with the collective intelligence of past labor (including, if they’re lucky, some of the ideas produced by left-wing scholars, activists, organizers, and unionists). Of course, education should never be treated as “a simple matter of rote knowledge transmission,” with “experts passing information to non-experts by whatever medium is available.” [60] This is why the struggle against chatbots is a struggle over not only the content of education, but its form . There was, to be sure, nothing utopian about US colleges and universities before chatbots were unleashed. [61] At the nominally “public” research university where I work, market and administrative logics dominate. Despite what the mission statement would like you to believe, managers seem to care more about serving military-industrial interests than the public good. [62] Nationwide, higher ed is “a profoundly conservative place where its senior managers toe the line of whatever political flavor governments, businesses, and wealthy donors desire.” [63] Sixty percent of my university’s total revenue comes from tuition dollars. Meanwhile, Blackstone’s “campus entrepreneurship program” has a glassy office on the main floor of the student union building. A recent email from the university president announced the hiring of a new, so-called “CEO” to run one of our state’s two-year colleges, which boasts “workforce partnerships” with the Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses program and the Berkshire Hathaway Energy (BHE) Foundation. In their 2026 Corporate Overview, BHE confirmed plans to “support the expansion of new large-load industries, such as data centers,” [64] even as parts of Montana experienced record-high temperatures and record-low snowpack levels this year, with knock-on effects for wildlife, agriculture, and wildfire risk, as well as for people who work outdoors or in buildings without air conditioning. [65] (Hence Ben Tarnoff’s claim that “to decarbonize, we must decomputerize.”) [66] A foam board display in the campus library — part of MSU-Bozeman’s efforts to solicit feedback on its new “ Strategic Plan .” Photo by the author. Nor is it a secret that the majority of college teachers have, for decades, been overworked, underpaid, short-term contract workers. College students, in many cases, are no better off: those lucky enough to even get admitted are often burdened by debt, struggling to balance school with work and family obligations, and increasingly disabled by the debilitating stress associated with high-pressure competitive capitalism, “a social order that appears to be waiting for them to make mistakes, to fall, and to be replaced by someone worthier.” [67] Chatbots only add insult to injury, exploiting students’ and teachers’ precarity and their understandable desire for (seemingly) cheap, quick shortcuts that short-circuit the slower, messier, embodied process of human-centric reflection, judgment, and analysis. (According to a 2025 AAUP report, “preexisting work intensification and devaluation” of things like responding to emails, writing rec letters, making slideshows, and designing new course syllabi “are the main reasons respondents give for using AI to assist with academic tasks.”) [68] Thus, the problem is not just the lack of public, democratic ownership and control; the problem is also that chatbots (and the social relations they presuppose) estrange people from themselves, others, and nature by depriving us of (1) the capacity to make informed judgments based on good reasons and reliable evidence, and (2) the capacity to forge empathetic connections with one another by imagining how and why another person (not a machine) holds a particular set of beliefs, values, and perspectives. The work of making and using chatbots should therefore be viewed as “ inhuman labor, since it denies the realization of distinctively human capacities.” [69] This doesn’t mean that there’s some essential, authentic human nature that we need to protect or recover, which would be out of step with autonomist Marxism’s concerns with collective self-invention rather than individual self-restoration. [70] It means that chatbots seem to be one of the things that severely stifle our distinctive capacity for collective self-invention. Unlike AI text, human-generated text is a uniquely formidable “technology for constructing options” and imagining alternatives. [71] This is one reason why Big Tech is so intent on making language as “vague, mechanical, unthinking, [and] endlessly univocal” as possible. [72] To deny the inherently class-conflictual aspects of language and meaning only makes it that much easier for schools to play their assigned role as places “where the contradic­tions between what capitalism promises and what it actually delivers are normalized.” [73] The AI industry is selling us an alienated, anti-democratic vision of language and education (and social relations generally). It’s not a vision in which knowledge, information, and education are universally accessible, but a vision in which knowledge, information, and education are considered obsolete and unnecessary. If Gorz and Marx are right about how capitalist production “not only creates an object for the subject, but also a subject for the object” [74] — in this case, a subject who’s been rendered so helpless that a chatbot feels helpful — then we need new, eco-socialist ways of thinking (and chatting) about human needs. eco-socialist reskilling To effectively, collectively heal the injuries described above (not just the insults) and develop our stifled communicative and imaginative capacities, there’s clearly an urgent need for cross-sector solidarity among workers of all kinds: productive and reproductive, paid and unpaid. [75] The question, as always, is what kind of political glue can hold them all together. For green syndicalist Jeff Shantz, the answer is health and safety — a transnational version of OSHA, more or less, that applies to both work environments and living environments: Assuming that workers do not prefer to poison themselves and their families, the ecological health of workers’ communities provides for an immediate barometer of democracy in the productive sphere, where effects become personalized in the community or even in the body . . . Against processes of deskilling, indeed as a specific reskilling outside of mere job performance, health and safety efforts suggest a possible transcending of the ‘expert elitism’ [identified by some] as a serious inhibition to efforts of democratization . . . [as] workers learn about what goes into their bodies, their homes, and their neighborhood.” [76] How to accomplish this? In many places, it’s already happening. Around the world, “the class struggle of production is converging with class-based environmental justice struggles over food, air, water, and the conditions of social and ecological reproduction,” as eco-Marxist sociologist John Bellamy Foster observes. [77] One way for socialists to make strategic, political use of this convergence is to acknowledge that resisting Promethean, productivist machine logics in the present can be a necessary (if also insufficient) part of what Foster calls “the long ecological revolution,” led by an “environmental proletariat” who refuses to be a passive victim of technological change. [78] The list below is inspired by some of these efforts, which could be described not only as efforts to “struggle for human autonomy from capital” but also “to struggle for a recognition of the ecological and cosmic human enmeshments and imbrications that capital obscures and obliterates.” [79] Some promising ways to make time and space for new, cooperative, autonomous forms of political, economic, and ecological literacy include the following: join and strengthen networks like the Tech Workers Coalition, [80] the Trade Unions for Energy Democracy coalition, [81] and the Blue-Green Alliance, [82] and campaigns like the National Council for Occupational Safety and Health (COSH)’s Fired Up! Workers for Heat Justice campaign [83] conduct and circulate collaborative, experiential “workers’ inquiries” of the kind described in Notes from Below Issue 27, Workers’ Inquiry: The Politics of a Method and on Long-Haul ’s About page support democratic economic planning efforts, [84] such as by developing sector-specific, digital-era Lucas Plans (the original Combine Committee’s Lucas Plan was nominated for the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize and demanded, among other things, “human skills-based production rather than automation,” [85] re-orienting arms production toward more socially useful products, and “re-organizing work into less hierarchical teams that bridged divisions between tacit knowledge on the shop floor and theoretical engineering knowledge in design shops”) [86] organize informal, in-person study groups and teach-ins using documentaries like The Story of the Lucas Aerospace Shop Stewards Alternative Corporate Plan , [87] podcasts like Tech Won’t Save Us , and texts like the 2010 Cochabamba People’s Agreement, [88] the Labor Network for Sustainability’s 2021 “Just Transition Listening Project” report; [89] the 2023 Common Ecologies booklet, Towards Agroecological Futures: How to Facilitate Local Agroecological Transitions ; [90] the AAUP’s collection of AI resources (including How to Use FOIA to Uncover Higher Ed Partnerships and Contracts with Tech Companies ); [91] the UC Berkeley Labor Center’s collection of tech-related CBA language, “Negotiating Tech: An Inventory of U.S. Union Contract Provisions for the Digital Age”; [92] Richard Lewontin’s 1998 book, The Triple Helix: Gene, Organism, and Environment ; Victor Wallis’s 2018 book, Red-Green Revolution: The Politics and Technology of Ecosocialism ; or Ellen David Friedman’s 2026 book Keep Going: A Guide to Organizing When It’s Hard organize for not only the elimination of no-strike contract clauses [93] but also for the repeal (and/or mass violation) of your state’s version of Montana’s absurdly expansive “Management Rights of Public Employers” law, which among other things protects an employer’s right to “establish the methods and processes by which work is performed” (often broadly interpreted to apply to the unilateral imposition of new technology) [94] lobby for a federal jobs guarantee, a federal heat standard, [95] a robot tax, [96] a global Green New Deal, a 32-hour work week, an international phase-out of fossil fuels, [97] and a “renewed, permanent” Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) [98] initiate and/or support a building trades version of the Tech Won’t Build It movement [99] that’s directed at large-scale data centers (the Montana AFL-CIO’s recently passed “Resolution on Data Centers, AI, and a Worker-Centered Economy” — jointly submitted by the Montana State Building & Construction Trades Council and the Montana Nurses Association — is unfortunately marred by a commitment to meritocracy and productivism: the resolution opposes a moratorium on data center construction, treating a growing “digital economy” as basically inevitable and claiming that “more demand” for supposedly job-creating data centers to become “part of critical infrastructure” will help labor unions “deliver on the promise of the American Dream” and “grow the middle class” — the resolution fails to mention that capitalists, not workers, are the ones driving this demand) [100] use, create, or participate in user- and worker-controlled “platform coops,” decentralized forms of “peer-to-peer production,” [101] community makerspaces, and AI-free search tools like NoAI.duckduckgo.com sign and share the Open Letter from Educators Who Refuse the Call to Adopt GenAI in Education ; make and share your own, institution-specific version of the SUNY Oswego AI Opt Out petition ; and join informal networks like the Alliance for Refusing Generative Artificial Intelligence Discord server , which as of this writing has more than 400 users (many of them are college writing teachers, but not all) initiate and/or support large-scale, coordinated data poisoning, server overloads, and other “strategic disruptions” of the digital economy’s logistical chokepoints [102] (to the extent that chatbots can be used to sabotage chatbots, they could in fact be considered a means of struggle) [103] The upshot of all this is that a genuinely sustainable, participatory economy requires forms of communication and cooperation that are incompatible with the alienating, labor-intensive, neo-Taylorist chatbot technologies marketed as “generative AI.” “Real collective decision-making about fourth industrial revolution technologies must include the possibility of roads not taken, and humans rejecting the liquidation of their activities by machinic intelligence,” as the authors of Inhuman Power: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Capitalism rightly insist. [104] Here’s my AI policy for this semester’s course syllabi, if any readers are curious. Instead of taking a punitive, disciplinary approach, my goal is to raise awareness about these tools’ flaws, limitations, and enabling conditions, inviting students to share their own questions and experiences. My goal, in other words, is to teach them the things about chatbots that they could never learn from chatbots themselves. Such as the fact that people don’t use chatbots; rather, chatbots use people. To be honest, it did occur to me that I could finish this essay a lot earlier if I used a chatbot, potentially “saving” me hundreds of hours (read: outsourcing hundreds of hours) of reading, writing, and revising (not to mention hundreds of ounces of Folger’s and Hamm’s). Even after all that time and effort, I’m still not entirely happy with the result. But there’s no quicker, easier way. Nor should there be. The revolution will not be outsourced! Indeed, if socialism means, among other things, the end of class (i.e., not just working-class self-emancipation but self-abolition ), then we must refuse to act, whenever possible, as if human labor-power is an abstract, interchangeable entity — that is, a commodity. Universal fungibility, after all, is one of the foundational lies of capitalism, and one that chatbots perpetuate: a denial of qualitative differences among concrete objects and activities, and the related insistence that mechanization can increase economic quantities without transforming (or sacrificing) social and environmental qualities. Whether mechanization-induced tradeoffs are worth it must always be decided by those who’ll be affected the most. That temptation to turn to a chatbot was a revealing one, though. However structurally alienating, inadequate, and unreliable they might be, chatbots do respond to legitimate wants and needs — especially the desire for free, universal, instantaneous access to meaningful assistance of various kinds, from counseling and tutoring to programming, graphic design, Wikipedia-style informational overviews, or even just basic companionship. Unfortunately, in lieu of real socialism — which would require, among other things, free, universal access to high-quality, person-centered education — capital has given us simulated socialism: global access to a virtual, text-centered army of over-eager Stepford professionals, as the contrasting images below demonstrate: An email ad from OpenAI, and a flyer in the campus library. Photo by the author. Maybe this is the real reason so many of us have been conditioned to think of chatbots as useful, even comforting. They try so hard to tell us the things capitalism doesn’t allow us to hear from actual people. They give us a taste — always only a taste — of another world. A world where the means of survival — including the means of acquiring political, economic, and ecological literacy — are no longer privatized, monopolized, and depersonalized. A world where social decision-making is no longer opaque, unaccountable, concentrated in the hands (and data centers) of a powerful few. A world where chatbots are no longer wanted or needed. Chatbots undermine these survival literacies, so we must undermine chatbots.
